```{r}
#| label: create-functions

run_replication <- function(replication, model) {
  set.seed(410000L + replication)
  population <- create_baseline_population(params$initial_population, 60, 2000, 
    group_weights = c("A" = 1, "B" = 1, "C" = 1))
  model <- model |> set_population(population)
  time <- system.time(result <- simulate(model, params$years, 420000L + replication))[["elapsed"]]
  result$runtime <- time
  return(result)
}
```

## Purpose and completion criteria


Assess whether the current simulation successfully handles time varying rate schedules and time varying model parameters. 


| Measure | Comparison | Acceptance criterion |
|---|---|---|
| TFR | Over time | Should change in the expected way over time within simulation and remain close to expected values |
| Life Expectancy at birth | Over time | Should change in the expected way over time within simulation and remain close to expected values |
| Accounting and implementation | Existing tests | Successful unit tests |

## Overview of Design

### Time-varying rate processes

For all rate processes, we add time varying rates by allowing stratification of these rate objects by `time_start` and `time_end` columns. The simulation will use the rates in the currect time interval as it progresses through time in the simulation. If the `time_start` and `time_end` columns are not provided, then the rates will remain constant throughout the simulation. Users can use `Inf` in `time_end` to indicate a time interval that should be followed for the remainder of the simulation.

The times provided must cover the entire interval of the simulation and there can be no gaps. If the program detects a lack of coverage or gaps, it will fail to process the simulation with an error. This requires some extra work by the user to ensure that they providing adequate coverage. Notably, you can provide time intervals that exceed the coverage without problem.For example, you could provide historical fertility rates from 1900 to 2000 and then run the simulation only from 1950 to 1980. This makes it possible for users to download large historical rate schedules and use them without further modification to fit a specific time period, so long as the simulation time period falls within the range.

It is also possible for users to create time varying rates by stopping the simulation and then restarting it with the final results from the previous simulation and new rates. However, because there is some initialization cost to each simulation, this approach will usually be *substantially* slower than specifying time-varying rates within a single simulation.

The argument to `cohab_prob`, while not technically a rate, takes the same form as a rate process and so we allow it to vary in the same way.

To assist with generating long runs of rates, the `get_mortality_hmd` and `get_fertility_hfd` functions have been improved to pull in a vector of years rather than just a single year. Additionally, users can specify age by time shapes other than 1x1 with the `shape` argument to `get_mortality_hmd` (the only shape currently available in HFD is 1x1).

### Time-varying matching and inheritance models

The matching models used in the union formation process (assigned by arguments `matching`, `cohab_matching`, and `father_matching`) and the inheritance models used in the fertility process are additional places where users may wish to add time variance within a single simulation. For example, users may wish to adjust the rate of exogamy between groups over time, shift preferences in spousal age differences, or shift to a difference method for inheritance of group identity.

To specify time variance, these arguments can be entered as tibbles that include the `time_start` and `time_end` columns as well as a list column for the `model`. So for example:

```r
tibble(
  time_start = c(1950, 1980),
  time_end   = c(1980, Inf),
  model      = list(
    create_age_gap_matching_model(2, 5),
    create_age_gap_matching_model(4, 5)
  )
)
```

will create two separate matching models that differ by the preferred spousal age gap. From 1950 until 1980, the first model will be used and from 1980 onward, the second model will be used.

The arguments for both matching and inheritance will take either a single model for time constant models or a time-varying tibble of this format.

## Inputs and Simulation Design

For this milestone, I am going to try several different demonstration projects with time-varying rates in some capacity to show off the full range of the program at this point. I will define inputs within each demonstration project.

Rather than Monte Carlo replication, I will focus on a single simulation with a large initial population and I will use visual examination to confirm that rates are changing at the appropriate point and the confidence intervals around rates themselves at selected time points to confirm that the input rates are being preserved correctly. Confidence intervals are defined by the correct Poisson confidence interval around each rate, which can account better for sparse cells than the normal approximation.

## Demonstration Projects

### The Demographic Transition

I will reproduce the demographic transition by using fertility and mortality rates for Sweden, available from th Human Fertility Database (HFD) and Human Mortality Database (HMD). 

Age-specific fertility rates in Sweden only go back to 1891, while age-specific mortality rates go back to 1751. both series continue until 2024. I will download the full range of years for each series. In some cases, using the full open age of 110+ from the HMD can lead to missing values at extreme ages in older dat, so I truncate the open-age group to 95 (this is done correctly by recomputing the open-age mortality rate by pooling deaths and person years for that inteval from HMD data).

```{r}
#| label: get-rates-demog-trans-sweden

fertility_rates_sweden <- get_fertility_hfd("SWE", 1891:2024)
mortality_rates_sweden <- get_mortality_hmd("SWE", 1751:2024, open_age = 95)
```

The mortality transition was already well underway by 1891, when we first get the fertility data, so I will make the assumption that fertility rates before 1891 were at the 1891 levels.

I want to start the simulation with a population age structure fom a stable but stationary population. To do so, I need to find mortality rates to match with the 1891 fertility rates that will produce roughly zero population growth in the stable population. I use the approximation that:

$$r = \log(NRR)/\mu$$

Where $\mu$ is the mean age of childbearing. I test different candidate years until I get one that works in the code below.

```{r}
#| label: determine-growth-rate-zero
#| eval: false

get_growth_rate <- function(fert_rates, mort_rates) {

  NRR <- mort_rates |> calculate_life_table() |>
    filter(sex == "f") |>
    select(age_start, Lx) |>
    right_join(fert_rates, by = c("age_start")) |>
    mutate(prod = Lx * rate) |>
    pull(prod) |>
    sum() * 0.4886
  mu <- sum((fert_rates$age_start + 0.5) * fert_rates$rate) / sum(fert_rates$rate)

  log(NRR)/mu

}

fert_rates <- fertility_rates_sweden |> filter(time_start == 1891)
get_growth_rate(fert_rates, mortality_rates_sweden |> filter(time_start == 1810))
get_growth_rate(fert_rates, mortality_rates_sweden |> filter(time_start == 1812))
get_growth_rate(fert_rates, mortality_rates_sweden |> filter(time_start == 1813))
get_growth_rate(fert_rates, mortality_rates_sweden |> filter(time_start == 1838))
get_growth_rate(fert_rates, mortality_rates_sweden |> filter(time_start == 1811))
```

Mortality rates in 1811 are the winner. Pairing them with the 1891 fertility rates gives me a growth rate of 0.0019 per annum.

The next task is to run a 100 year simulation from a uniform population distribution to produce my starting stationary population. To do this correctly, I want to start this simulation 100 years before when I want to start my "real" simulation. I decide on 1780 as a starting point for my simulation. 

```{r}
#| label: get-starting-stationary-pop

fert_rates <- fertility_rates_sweden |> filter(time_start == 1891) |>
  select(-starts_with("time_"))
mort_rates <- mortality_rates_sweden |> filter(time_start == 1811) |>
  select(-starts_with("time_"))

pop <- create_baseline_population(100000, 70, 1780 - 100)
model <- hammel_model() |>
  set_population(pop) |>
  set_fertility(fert_rates) |>
  set_mortality(mort_rates) |>
  set_union_formation("on_demand")
pop_start <- simulate(model, 100, 1)
```

I now have a starting population that should be roughly consistent with the stable population under Sweden's pre-transition rates. I can now use my time-varying rates to project this population forward. I will project it to 2020. Since I only care about the effect of fertility and mortality rates on creating the demographic transition, I will use the "on demand" model for union formation and will not complicate the simulation otherwise.

```{r}
#| label: run-simulation-demog-transition

# for fertiliity rates I need to extend the last year back to my starting point of 1870
# I do this by adding one row at the front for the 1780-1891 time period that duplicates 
# my 1891 rates
fertility_rates_sweden <- bind_rows(
  fertility_rates_sweden |>
    filter(time_start == 1891) |>
    mutate(time_start = 1780, time_end = 1891),
  fertility_rates_sweden
)

model <- hammel_model() |>
  set_population(pop_start) |>
  set_fertility(fertility_rates_sweden) |>
  set_mortality(mortality_rates_sweden) |>
  set_union_formation("on_demand")
sim_time_demog_trans <- system.time(pop_final <- simulate(model, 2020 - 1780, 1))
```

The simulation took `r sim_time_demog_trans` seconds to run.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pop-size-demog-trans
#| fig-cap: Relative population size from start from simulation starting in 1780 to 2020, using Sweden's historic age-specific fertility and mortality rates

pop_final |> calculate_population_size(1780:2020) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = population / first(population)))+
  geom_line()+
  labs(x = "year", y = "population size relative to initial")
```

@fig-pop-size-demog-trans show the population size over time in the simulation. It displays the classic S-shaped curve expected of the demographic transition, although we start late enough in 1780 that it is already rising a bit at the beginning. The population grows by four-fold over the simulation period. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-crude-rates-demog-trans
#| fig-cap: Crude birth and death rates annually over the simulation

births <- pop_final$persons |>
  mutate(year = floor(birth_time)) |>
  count(year, name = "births")
deaths <- pop_final$persons |>
  mutate(year = floor(death_time)) |>
  count(year, name = "deaths")
crude_rates <- calculate_population_size(pop_final, 1780:2019 + 0.5) |>
  mutate(year = floor(time)) |>
  left_join(births, by = "year") |>
  left_join(deaths, by = "year") |>
  mutate(rate_birth = births / population, rate_death = deaths / population) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("rate_"), names_prefix = "rate_",
               names_to = "event", values_to = "crude_rate") 

crude_rates |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = crude_rate, color = event))+
  geom_line()+
  labs(x = "year", y = "crude rate")
```

@fig-crude-rates-demog-trans shows another classic demographic transition figure - A comparison of crude birth and death rates over time. These are estimated by taking counts of births or deaths over mid-yer population sizes. Mortality rates fall faster than fertility rates over the time period, leading to population growth. We can also see the post-war baby boom.

```{r}
#| label: fig-tfr-demog-trans
#| fig-cap: Total fertility rates by year of the simulation. Dotted red line shows the total fertility rate from the input rates.

input_tfr <- fert_rates_time |> calculate_tfr()

calculate_fertility_rates(pop_final, 1780:2020, 12:55) |> 
  calculate_tfr() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time_start, y = tfr))+
  geom_line()+
  geom_line(data = input_tfr, linetype = 2, color = 'red')+
  labs(x = "year", y = "total fertility rate")
```

@fig-tfr-demog-trans shows the estimated TFR for each year of the simulation. The dotted red line shows the TFR from the input rates. The estimated TFRs match closely to that expected by the input rates. There is less random noise at the end of the simulation when the population is much larger.

```{r}
#| label: fig-life-exp-demog-trans
#| fig-cap: Life expectancy at age zero by year of the simulation, separately by gender. Dotted red lines show the life expectancy at birth from input rates.

input_lifeexp <- mort_rates_time |> calculate_life_table() |>
  # 1853 has a problem with the open-ended age caegory leading to Inf results so remove it
  filter(age_start == 0, time_start != 1853)

calculate_mortality_rates(pop_final, 1780:2020, 0:85) |>
  calculate_life_table() |>
  filter(age_start == 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time_start, y = ex))+
  geom_line()+
  geom_line(data = input_lifeexp, linetype = 2, color = 'red')+
  facet_wrap(~sex)+
  labs(x = "year", y = "life expectancy at birth")
```

@fig-life-exp-demog-trans shows the estimated life expectancy at birth for each year of the simulation. The dotted red line shows the life expectancy at birth from the input rates. The estimated life expectancy matches closely to that expected by the input rates.

As a final test, I look at age-specific mortality rates and age-specific fertility rates at specific time points and compare them to the input rates at those time points. For this exercise I also show the 95% CI around each of my estimates.

```{r}
#| label: fig-asfr-demog-trans
#| fig-cap: Age-specific fertility rates estimated from simulation for selected years. 95% confidence band shown around each estimate. Dotted red line shows input rate.

selected_years <- c(1900, 1920, 1940, 1960, 1980, 2000)
temp <- fertility_rates_sweden |>
  filter(time_start %in% selected_years)

calculate_fertility_rates(pop_final, 1780:2020, 12:55, conf.level = 0.95) |>
  filter(time_start %in% selected_years) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = age_start + 0.5, y = rate_fertility))+
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf_low, ymax = conf_high), color = NA, fill = "grey70")+
  geom_point(size = 0.5)+
  geom_line(data = temp, aes(y = rate), linetype = 2, color = "red")+
  facet_wrap(~time_start)+
  labs(x = "age", y = "age-specific fertility rate")
```

@fig-asfr-demogr-trans shows the estimated fertility rates at 20 year intervals from 1900 to 2000. Dotted red lines show the values from the input rates. The red dotted line fits well to the estimated data and is generally within the 95% confidence interval. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-asmr-demog-trans
#| fig-cap: Age-specific mortality rates by sex estimated from simulation for selected years. 95% confidence band shown around each estimate. Dotted red line shows input rate.

selected_years <- c(1800, 1850, 1900, 1950, 2000)
temp <- mortality_rates_sweden |>
  filter(time_start %in% selected_years)

calculate_mortality_rates(pop_final, 1780:2020, 0:95, conf.level = 0.95) |>
  filter(time_start %in% selected_years) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = age_start + 0.5, y = rate_mortality))+
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf_low, ymax = conf_high), color = NA, fill = "grey70")+
  geom_point(size = 0.5)+
  geom_line(data = temp, aes(y = rate), linetype = 2, color = "red")+
  facet_grid(sex~time_start)+
  scale_y_log10()+
  labs(x = "age", y = "age-specific mortality rate")
```

@fig-asmr-demogr-trans shows the estimated mortality  rates at 50 year intervals from 1800 to 2000. Dotted red lines show the values from the input rates. In the more recent years, very low mortality rates at some younger ages lead to no observed deaths in some single year age groups, resulting in wide confidence bands. In general, the red dotted line fits well to the estimated data and is generally within the 95% confidence interval.
